The fog did not roll in; it arrived. It pressed against the granite cliffs of Blackrock Point like a living thing, heavy and suffocating, smelling of salt, ozone, and something older—something that smelled like wet stone and forgotten time.

Elias Thorne adjusted the brass railing of the gallery deck, his knuckles white against the cold iron. He was not the first keeper of the Blackrock Light. In fact, if you asked the historian in the port town of Oakhaven, they would tell you there had been twelve keepers since the lighthouse was built in 1892. They would give you names: Arthur Penhaligon, Silas Vane, Martha Halloway, and so on, up to number twelve, who had vanished in 1974 along with his family.

But Elias was not number twelve.

He was number zero.

The plaque on the door of the keeper’s cottage read *Lighthouse Keeper: 0*. It was a mistake, the locals said. A clerical error from the early days when the registry wasn’t digital, or perhaps a joke played by a drunken municipal clerk. But Elias knew better. He knew because the previous keeper, Arthur Penhaligon, had told him before he died, in a voice that sounded like grinding gravel: *"You don’t keep the light, boy. You keep the door."*

Elias pulled his wool coat tighter. The wind howled, a mournful sound that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere. He climbed the 144 spiral steps to the lantern room, his boots echoing on the cast-iron grating. The Fresnel lens, a towering beehive of prisms and glass, sat in the cente

The sea does not forgive. It does not remember names, nor does it care for the history written in ink or stone. It only cares for the rhythm of its own breathing, the endless, heaving inhalation and exhalation that has defined the edge of the world for millennia.

And at the very edge of that world, where the Atlantic Ocean crashes against the jagged teeth of the Rock of Aethelgard, stood the Lighthouse of the Void.

Inside its highest chamber, amidst the smell of ozone, kerosene, and old paper, sat Keeper #0.

He was not the first keeper. That title belonged to a man named Silas, who had arrived three centuries ago with a lantern and a prayer. Silas had been followed by Keeper #1, then #2, and so on, up to Keeper #99, who had vanished during the Great Storm of 1982, leaving behind only a half-eaten sandwich and a logbook entry that read: *The light is blinking in Morse code. It says: "Come down."*

But Keeper #0 was different. He had no predecessor. He had no number in the official registry, because the registry had been burned in a fire that started with no spark. He was the anomaly, the glitch in the bureaucratic machinery of the Maritime Authority, the man who had simply appeared one Tuesday morning, sitting in the chair that had been empty for forty years, polishing the brass fittings of the Fresnel lens with a rag that looked like it was made of moonlight.
